text.content:
This part follows a fight from the first initiative to the last bandage: who acts when, how to shoot, throw a grenade or strike, how to defend and resist damage, then how to heal, poison or detox, and finally how to pick someone's pockets or run. Each chapter can be read on its own; the GM and the player each find in it the gestures that concern them.

One principle runs through the whole part: almost everything is played from the previous chat card. The attack sets the defense button, the defense sets the resistance button, the resistance the damage button. Before attacking, target your opponent (@UUID[Compendium.sr5.manual.JournalEntry.UtP5ShuRjXa3JrEZ.JournalEntryPage.9jXWevgNpySvo7Wz]{the token HUD}): without a target, the card has nobody to offer the response to.

What it is for

In Shadowrun, a fast character acts several times per Combat Turn, and each action they spend is counted down (Core Rulebook p. 159-162). Foundry's encounter tracker does it for you: it orders the combatants by Initiative Score, moves from one Initiative Pass to the next, and keeps for each the count of their Free, Simple and Complex Actions. The GM keeps control: they correct a counter with a click, give a character back their actions, and choose how far the system enforces the rule.

Step by step: starting a combat (GM)

  1. Select the combatants' tokens, right-click one of them and click Toggle Combat State: they join the scene's encounter.

  2. Open the Combat tab of the sidebar (the two crossed swords).

  3. Click Roll All (the group icon, ①) or Roll NPCs, right next to it, if the players roll themselves. Each rolls the initiative that matches what they are doing: physical, astral or Matrix, the system chooses on its own.

  4. Click Begin Encounter. The first Initiative Pass opens (②) and the combatant with the highest score (④) takes the lead.

  5. When a combatant has finished, click Next Turn (the arrow at the bottom right of the tracker).

Hovering over a line of the tracker highlights the combatant's token, without opening its PAN crown. Each line's initiative die turns red on hover. A combatant the GM hides stays in the GM's list, greyed, at its place in the turn order; the players do not see it. On the scene, the token of the combatant who has the lead carries the system's turn marker, DjamZ's ouroboros; a marker chosen in Foundry's combat settings takes precedence over it.

Backlinks: @UUID[.v1sy6q1A3WbLzLob]{MENU}

@UUID[.vdqzSQJsSq8mvqKb]{Initiative Passes} →

Under the turn number (Foundry's Round), the tracker shows the current Initiative Pass. When everyone has played, the system opens the next pass (Core Rulebook p. 160):

  • it subtracts 10 from each Initiative Score;

  • only the combatants whose score stays above 0 act again; the others have finished their Combat Turn;

  • it gives their actions back to those who act again;

  • it counts down the effects whose duration is counted in passes.

At the next Combat Turn, initiative is rolled again and the previous turn's Edge expenses are forgotten. Each new turn also moves the world's clock forward by three seconds (Core Rulebook p. 49) (@UUID[Compendium.sr5.manual.JournalEntry.UtP5ShuRjXa3JrEZ.JournalEntryPage.YRfJG9p6WnN6cUDi]{the clock}).

Backlinks: @UUID[.v1sy6q1A3WbLzLob]{MENU} > @UUID[.IUNfbsSb66lrAYLT]{3.1 Initiative and actions}

← @UUID[.IUNfbsSb66lrAYLT]{3.1 Initiative and actions} · @UUID[.C9Btmx4cbjNuoi7a]{Action counters} →

On each line of the tracker, three figures (③): from left to right the Free, Simple and Complex Actions the combatant has left in the pass. They go down on their own when the character acts from their sheet: a shot takes a Simple Action, a spell a Complex Action, and a notification says what was taken and why.

Simple and Complex are linked: per pass, you are entitled to two Simple Actions or one Complex Action, plus one Free Action (Core Rulebook p. 162). A Simple Action spent therefore removes the Complex Action, and a Complex Action removes both Simple ones.

Step by step: correcting a counter (GM)

  1. Click a figure to remove one action of that type.

  2. Hold Shift and click to give one back.

The system notes that the adjustment is manual. To give everything back at once, go through the right-click menu (below).

What a few gestures cost

GestureCost in combat
Firing single shot or semi-automatic, throwing a weapona Simple Action (Core Rulebook p. 165)
Firing a burst or full auto, attacking in melee, sprintinga Complex Action (Core Rulebook p. 167)
Casting a spell, using a skill in your own phasea Complex Action (Core Rulebook p. 167)
Switching a device's wirelessa Free Action (Core Rulebook p. 163); a Simple Action without a direct neural interface if the GM requires it (setting below) (Core Rulebook p. 165)
Reloading, removing a clipdepending on the weapon and the clip, per the book's table (Core Rulebook p. 167)
Rebooting your device from the sheeta Complex Action
Runninga Free Action per pass in which you move at a run (Core Rulebook p. 162) (@UUID[.AHFI77k4yz9xyzT4]{running})
Defending, resisting damage or a spellnothing: it is not an action
A Perception asked for by the GM during someone else's phasenothing: it is a reaction

Outside combat, nothing is counted down: activating a focus, switching a wireless or rebooting before the fight does not lower the counters.

NPCs with unlinked tokens: play from the token

The sheet opened from the actors tab is the base actor's, which is none of its tokens: its rolls do not count down actions and do not touch initiative. For a guard, a ganger or any NPC in several copies, open the sheet with a double click on its token.

pages.name: The combatant menu: Edge, delay, reset

text.content:
A right-click on a line of the tracker opens the combatant menu. The system adds its own entries to Foundry's.

  • Seize the initiative: the character goes to the head of the order; Blitz: their initiative is rerolled with five dice (Core Rulebook p. 161). Both cost a point of Edge, and the system refuses, saying so, when none is left.

  • -1, -5, -10 Initiative Score: to apply by hand a cost the system does not know.

  • Reset actions (GM only): the combatant gets back their Free Action, their two Simple and their Complex Action, as at the start of a pass.

  • Delaying action: the combatant leaves the order and takes the lead again when they decide (Core Rulebook p. 161).

Backlinks: @UUID[.v1sy6q1A3WbLzLob]{MENU} > @UUID[.IUNfbsSb66lrAYLT]{3.1 Initiative and actions}

← @UUID[.C9Btmx4cbjNuoi7a]{Action counters} · @UUID[.zazYeX6j2LJUFITG]{What costs initiative} →

Some choices do not take an action but Initiative points, which the tracker removes at once (Core Rulebook p. 168):

ChoiceCost
Full defense (box in the defense window)−10
Active defense: dodge, block, parrydepending on the defense (@UUID[.IwEisvMqg55fA2Ez]{defending})
Interrupt Actionusually −5, sometimes −10

Full defense and active defense are paid together: the score must exceed their combined cost, strictly (11 or more for full defense alone). Two interrupts played in a single gesture add their costs. When the score is not enough, the system refuses the choice and says which of the two figures is short.

Wounds lower the Initiative Score by their modifier, once per wound, and give it back when they heal (Core Rulebook p. 169). For the hacker who interrupts an action thanks to a Watchdog mark, see @UUID[Compendium.sr5.manual.JournalEntry.CKM0UvZC23LLnCgv.JournalEntryPage.lDEaMIJ23r49haVj]{the radial menu}.

Backlinks: @UUID[.v1sy6q1A3WbLzLob]{MENU} > @UUID[.IUNfbsSb66lrAYLT]{3.1 Initiative and actions}

← @UUID[.9F7HzsqZCCyFgdfv]{The combatant menu: Edge, delay, reset} · @UUID[.AvygJ8SSoiLZHj5j]{The "Actions and initiative" lock (GM)} →

By default, the system follows the book: a Simple or Complex Action is played in your own phase (Core Rulebook p. 162), and a score of 0 or less only leaves a Free Action (Core Rulebook p. 160). What it does with an action the character no longer has is set in the Rule locks window.

Step by step: setting the actions lock

  1. Open Shadowrun settings (Settings tab, Configure Settings, Open the settings), Presets tab, then click Set the locks.

  2. Tick family by family yourself. To tick or untick everything at once, go through the Presets menu (@UUID[Compendium.sr5.manual.JournalEntry.arMGpK6RvbR3sLNQ.JournalEntryPage.MxHL8At1JidYvFM3]{see 8.1}).

  3. The Actions and initiative family (②) covers reloading without the necessary action, interrupting without enough initiative, parrying or blocking without the skill, and Edge during an extended test.

  4. The Block an action the character no longer has box (③) only targets missing actions: ticked, a Simple or Complex Action with no action available, or at 0 initiative or less, is refused without spending anything.

  5. Click Save.

An unticked family changes no computation: the action goes through, the counters go down as usual, and the GM gets a whisper, once per character and per Combat Turn. Outside your own phase, there is only ever a warning, even with the box ticked. The detail of the other families is in the chapter @UUID[Compendium.sr5.manual.JournalEntry.arMGpK6RvbR3sLNQ.JournalEntryPage.yj32FTBiKvVIyGIf]{on the rule locks}.

A new world asks the question once

On the first load of a new world, a window asks the GM for their automation: Advanced (the book, all boxes ticked), Light (everything unticked) or Custom (@UUID[Compendium.sr5.manual.JournalEntry.UtP5ShuRjXa3JrEZ.JournalEntryPage.Gfk5zUuTaOqS9vUv]{the first launch}). A world updated from an older version keeps the choice it had: box ③ stays unticked there.

Backlinks: @UUID[.v1sy6q1A3WbLzLob]{MENU} > @UUID[.IUNfbsSb66lrAYLT]{3.1 Initiative and actions}

← @UUID[.zazYeX6j2LJUFITG]{What costs initiative} · @UUID[.KgTwFfLYe1jWzYhd]{Run & Gun combat options (GM)} →

Run & Gun offers six rules to speed up or harden combat (Run & Gun p. 107-110). They are six world settings of the Combat tab, unticked by default as the book wants:

SettingTicked, the system…
RG1: no attack limit per Action Phasenotes the choice (the system already did not count attacks per phase).
RG2: target size modifiersadds or removes dice to the attack according to the target's Strength + Body (a troll at 20 gives +2 dice).
RG3: movement-based modifiersremoves dice from the attack against a character who moved, and from their own defense, according to the meters covered.
RG4: alternative initiativemakes the highest score act, which immediately loses 10; the order is redone after each action.
RG5: aiming for the gaps in armorremoves the target's armor (minus AP) from the attack pool, and no longer counts it when resisting damage.
RG6: increased damage against defenseless targetsincreases the DV when the defense pool drops below 0.

Each line appears in the attack or defense window when it applies, and stays editable. The detail: wiki: Initiative tracker (RG4).

Backlinks: @UUID[.v1sy6q1A3WbLzLob]{MENU} > @UUID[.IUNfbsSb66lrAYLT]{3.1 Initiative and actions}

← @UUID[.AvygJ8SSoiLZHj5j]{The "Actions and initiative" lock (GM)} · @UUID[.s7CPQ3PiwJNvuBmZ]{Squad maneuvers} →

A small trained team coordinates its moves through combat maneuvers: 11 from Run & Gun and 5 from Street Lethal (Run & Gun p. 98-104). The leader launches them from their Small Unit Tactics knowledge skill.

  1. On the leader's sheet, click the Small Unit Tactics knowledge skill: the Combat maneuver window opens.

  2. Choose the maneuver. The book's threshold is offered; the GM can set another one depending on the team's preparation (Run & Gun p. 99).

  3. Tick The team needs explanations (leader's complex action) if the maneuver is new: a Complex Action, Simple with a tactical network (TacNet) II or III (Run & Gun p. 104). Click Launch the maneuver.

  4. On the card, each member selects their token and clicks Join: Small Unit Tactics, or Intuition − 1 without the skill, plus the TacNet bonus. Then the leader rolls their Leader's test, with the teamwork bonus already counted (Core Rulebook p. 49).

The GM reads the result. Successful, the maneuver gives its bonus to all until the end of the Combat Turn; failed, all have a defense penalty for the pass, for the whole turn on a critical glitch. These bonuses and penalties arrive already ticked in the members' roll windows; the initiative of a maneuver and that of the tactical network (+5; +10 / +5 / +5) are added at once. End the maneuver removes its effects. The effects on opponents, surprise and counter-maneuvers are written on the card and stay with the GM.

Backlinks: @UUID[.v1sy6q1A3WbLzLob]{MENU} > @UUID[.IUNfbsSb66lrAYLT]{3.1 Initiative and actions}

← @UUID[.KgTwFfLYe1jWzYhd]{Run & Gun combat options (GM)} · @UUID[.H33zaMIqPXcJQeEh]{Related settings and references} →

What the system does on its own

  • It counts down the actions spent from the sheet, opens the passes and gives actions back to those who act again.

  • It removes the initiative cost of full defense, active defenses and interrupts, and the wound penalty.

  • It warns about an action played outside your phase or at 0 initiative, including for an NPC played by the GM.

What the GM does by hand

  • Enforces the countdown when the Block an action the character no longer has box is unticked.

  • Removes initiative for costs the system does not know (right-click menu) and decides on surprise.

← @UUID[.s7CPQ3PiwJNvuBmZ]{Squad maneuvers} · @UUID[.WCDbwwcR26uXK8o0]{3.2 Shooting} →

All

What it is for

A shot in Shadowrun depends on distance, light, fog, wind, what the shooter sees and the recoil of their weapon. The system measures the distance between the two tokens, reads the scene's conditions and the vision switched on in the sheet, counts bullets and recoil, then fills in the attack window: all you have left to do is check and roll.

Step by step: shooting an opponent

  1. Select your token, then target the opponent (right-click their token, then the target in the HUD, or the T key while hovering over it). One target at a time: with two, the shot is refused.

  2. Open your sheet at the weapons tab and click the figure in the weapon's DP (dice pool) column.

  3. The Attack with window opens, already filled in. Check the firing mode, range and modifiers; unfold a section by clicking its title to see the detail.

  4. Click Roll Dice. The attack card arrives in the chat with the Defend button for the target (@UUID[.IwEisvMqg55fA2Ez]{defending and resisting damage}).

Backlinks: @UUID[.v1sy6q1A3WbLzLob]{MENU}

← @UUID[.H33zaMIqPXcJQeEh]{Related settings and references} · @UUID[.zHEr1baI74LwUpuo]{Range} →

The system measures the distance with Foundry's ruler, converts it to meters (a scene in feet is understood), then compares it with the weapon's four ranges (Core Rulebook p. 185):

RangePenalty
Short—
Medium−1
Long−3
Extreme−6
Beyond extremeshot refused

The bounds are included: a target exactly 5 m from a heavy pistol is at short range. Firearms have fixed ranges; those of bows, crossbows and thrown weapons depend on the Strength of whoever holds them: read them on the weapon's sheet, they change from one character to another. In the window, the Range (combined with environment) line (③) offers the step measured; you can choose another.

What size of square?

The book's ranges are in meters: the system converts the scene's grid on its own. For a tactical map, keep Foundry's setting, 1.5 m per square (5 feet): it is what most commercial maps assume (@UUID[Compendium.sr5.manual.JournalEntry.arMGpK6RvbR3sLNQ.JournalEntryPage.ve0BXl53k8qhNxKU]{scenes}).

Backlinks: @UUID[.v1sy6q1A3WbLzLob]{MENU} > @UUID[.WCDbwwcR26uXK8o0]{3.2 Shooting}

← @UUID[.WCDbwwcR26uXK8o0]{3.2 Shooting} · @UUID[.PweWVX3c5dHC50Ul]{Light, visibility, wind} →

Each scene carries four conditions, which the GM sets in the scene's configuration.

Step by step: setting a scene's environment (GM)

  1. In the Scenes tab, right-click the scene and choose Configure.

  2. Open the Environmental Modifiers tab.

  3. Choose Visibility (①), Light (②), Glare (③) and Wind (④), then click Save Changes.

The system keeps the most penalizing condition, and goes up one step when several are equally severe (Core Rulebook p. 173). Range counts as one more condition: a medium range (−1) under partial light (−1) gives −3, not −2. The window keeps the Environmental Modifiers line (①) and only adds to the range line what range changes.

RollWhat counts
Shotvisibility, light and glare, wind, range
Defense against a shotvisibility, light and glare, as seen by the defender (neither wind nor range)
Meleevisibility, light and glare (not wind)
Visual Perceptionvisibility, light and glare

The scene read is the one displayed on screen. Light and glare form a single column of the table: the system takes the worse of the two, it does not add them.

Backlinks: @UUID[.v1sy6q1A3WbLzLob]{MENU} > @UUID[.WCDbwwcR26uXK8o0]{3.2 Shooting}

← @UUID[.zHEr1baI74LwUpuo]{Range} · @UUID[.u9jjBFVO4x8wpNs8]{What the shooter sees} →

Visions mostly soften the light line. The character switches them on themselves on their sheet, and their token immediately sees the scene differently.

Step by step: switching on a vision

  1. Open the sheet at the qualities tab: the Vision types block lists the visions the character has.

  2. Click the pin of the vision you want: it switches on and switches the others off. Natural vision (①) switches everything off and restores ordinary sight.

Vision onEffect on the modifiers
Low-light visionpartial and weak light count as full light; nothing in total darkness (Core Rulebook p. 175)
Thermographic visionlight and visibility go up one step: total darkness only costs −3 (Core Rulebook p. 175)
Ultrasoundlight raised by three steps, visibility by one
Astral perceptioneverything goes up four steps; switching to it costs a Simple Action

Cybereyes replace the metatype's vision: an elf with cybereyes loses their low-light vision, unless they bought it back as an enhancement (Core Rulebook p. 94). A flashlight mounted on the weapon only counts for shots made with that weapon: it provides partial light, and the low-light version brings total darkness down to −3 for those who see in dim light (Run & Gun p. 54). Switched on, it also dazzles the target of the shot: the target defends with at least a weak glare, if the light suits its vision, minus its flare compensation (Run & Gun p. 54, Core Rulebook p. 173). The detail of visions on the map, including ultrasound that pierces invisibility: wiki: Vision types.

The screen and the dice: two separate things

  • What Foundry shows depends on the light sources placed on the scene (lamps, ambient lights) and on the scene's darkness, a Foundry setting.

  • What the system counts for the dice are the conditions of the scene's Environmental Modifiers tab, corrected by the vision pinned on the sheet.

The two do not talk to each other: the darkness set in Foundry does not fill in the Light line of the rolls, and the Light line does not change the picture. Set both when you prepare a night scene.

VisionOn screen
Natural visionyou see what is lit; in complete darkness, nothing
Low-light visiondim light becomes full light: the weak halo of a lamp becomes as bright as its centre. In complete darkness, it changes nothing, on screen or with the dice (Core Rulebook p. 175, 444)
Thermographic visionsees heat, in the dark too, up to 30 m by default (adjustable)
Ultrasound"sees" shapes up to 50 m, reveals the invisible, stops at walls
Astral perceptiona greyed, bluish picture of the whole scene, up to 300 m by default, which shows auras; switching costs a Simple Action

"My low-light vision is useless"

On a fully dark scene, with no lamp at all, a samurai with low-light vision sees no better than anyone else: that is the rule, not a fault. Place a few weak lights (moon, distant neon, street lamps): low-light vision then has something to amplify.

  • A vision the character has but has not pinned gives neither the picture nor the dice correction.

  • An unlinked token only follows its own sheet: open the sheet from the token to pin its vision.

  • An Awakened character who perceives the astral also finds Astral Perception in the Vision types block: it is the same pin as in the Astral Plane block (@UUID[Compendium.sr5.manual.JournalEntry.jMw5X886fcLXtB6O.JournalEntryPage.DZqLEimyQwylLGta]{see 4.3}). For a spirit, it is always on (Core Rulebook p. 301).

Backlinks: @UUID[.v1sy6q1A3WbLzLob]{MENU} > @UUID[.WCDbwwcR26uXK8o0]{3.2 Shooting}

← @UUID[.PweWVX3c5dHC50Ul]{Light, visibility, wind} · @UUID[.SAu1crQUHZjeZLXE]{Firing modes, bursts and recoil} →

The Firing Mode list (②) only offers the weapon's modes: single shot, semi-automatic, semi-automatic burst, burst fire, full auto, suppressive fire (Core Rulebook p. 178-180). The number of bullets is written next to the mode, and the cost follows the book: Simple Action for single shot, semi-automatic and a short burst, Complex Action for long bursts and full auto (Core Rulebook p. 165, 167). Suppressive fire requires 20 bullets in the weapon (Core Rulebook p. 180).

Recoil builds up as long as the shooter does not stop firing (Core Rulebook p. 176): the Recoil line (④) shows the compensation of the weapon and accessories and the bullets already fired, and the pool shown takes it into account. It drops back to zero as soon as the shooter devotes an action to something else (Core Rulebook p. 176); the two-arrow icon, under the unfolded Recoil line, resets it by hand. Changing the firing mode in the window is paid when you shoot; closing the window without shooting costs nothing.

A shotgun also has the choke list (Choke settings): narrow, medium or wide spread (Core Rulebook p. 181). With no choice, the weapon is on narrow spread, as its sheet shows (the book gives no default, this is DjamZ's ruling). A flamethrower offers Fanning.

Weapon traits

On a weapon's sheet, a few traits change its figures by default:

  • Instrument of death: Accuracy −1, Availability +2, price doubled (No Future, p. 152-153).

  • Special modification (DV +1, AP −1, Accuracy +1, recoil compensation +1, Concealability −1, Reach +1): cumulative, for the Better Than Bad quality (Better Than Bad p. 161).

  • Net, XL net, ShockNet: the weapon throws a net (@UUID[.HxYeQa6b517Eo2te]{see 3.5}). The compendium's nets are recognized by their name.

Backlinks: @UUID[.v1sy6q1A3WbLzLob]{MENU} > @UUID[.WCDbwwcR26uXK8o0]{3.2 Shooting}

← @UUID[.u9jjBFVO4x8wpNs8]{What the shooter sees} · @UUID[.KDrTdedvj07yFm5y]{Ammunition and reloading} →

The sheet keeps count of bullets: each shot removes those of the chosen mode, and the system refuses a mode that requires more bullets than are left.

Step by step: reloading

  1. Keep ammunition of the right type on the sheet (Ammunition block, under the weapons).

  2. Click the two arrows (Reload Weapon) at the end of the weapon's line. The system draws on your ammunition and counts down the action the weapon requires.

  3. For a removable clip, a left click on the Ammo column inserts a clip, a right click removes it.

The cost follows the book's table (Core Rulebook p. 167): inserting or removing a clip, Simple Action; filling a clip, a cylinder or an internal magazine, Complex Action for (Agility) rounds; nocking an arrow, Simple Action. With the weapon's wireless on, removing the clip and changing the firing mode become Free Actions (Core Rulebook p. 425, 432); if the GM ticks Require a DNI to switch the wireless as a free action, only for a character linked by direct neural interface. A full weapon says so, and nothing is spent.

House Rules

Reload without spending an action (house rule), Combat tab of Shadowrun settings, unticked by default. Ticked, reloading in combat costs no action when ammunition of the right type is in the inventory, and filling a clip completely becomes possible. Removing a clip on its own keeps its cost.

All

What it is for

A grenade does not aim at an opponent: it aims at a point, and it can miss it. The system places on the scene a template the size of the blast, has the scatter die rolled when the thrower misses their landing point, moves the template that many meters in the right direction, then offers each person caught in the blast to resist, with damage that drops as you move away from the centre (Core Rulebook p. 181-183).

Step by step: throwing a grenade

  1. Select your token. On the sheet, weapons tab, click the grenade's dice pool (Grenades block).

  2. The blast template appears at the mouse pointer: bring it onto the target point and click the map to place it.

  3. The Attack with window opens: range is computed there from the thrower's Strength, as for a thrown weapon. Roll: it is Throwing Weapons + Agility [Physical], threshold 3, as a Simple Action (Core Rulebook p. 181).

  4. With 3 hits or more, the grenade lands where you wanted. Otherwise, the card carries the Scatter button: click it (next step by step).

  5. Each person caught in the blast clicks Take On Damage, with their own character selected; for NPCs, the GM selects their token. You do not defend against a blast: you resist it.

  1. Click Scatter on the throw's card (the thrower or the GM).

  2. The system rolls the distance, 1D6 meters minus hits for a standard grenade, and the direction on 2D6 on the book's diagram, oriented from the thrower towards the target point: a 7 goes beyond the target, a 2 or a 12 comes back towards the thrower (Core Rulebook p. 182).

  3. The template of this throw moves that many meters, and the card shows Scatter : N m.

At 0 hits, the grenade scatters the whole distance rolled. Scatter is counted in meters, not in squares: on a 1.5 m grid, 3 meters make two squares. Only whoever placed the template, or the GM, can scatter or remove it. If the template has been removed, resisting is refused: without a template, there is no point left to measure from.

What it is for

A melee attack is rolled like a shot, from the weapon's line, but it costs a Complex Action (Core Rulebook p. 167) and depends on reach rather than range. The system checks that the target is within arm's length, offers the melee modifiers and called shots, applies the martial arts techniques the character knows and, if the GM switches it on, tracks grappling: who holds whom, the hold's value and how to get out of it.

Step by step: striking an opponent

  1. Select your token and target the opponent, on a neighbouring square (or further if the weapon has reach).

  2. On the sheet, weapons tab, click the melee weapon's dice pool (Melee Weapons block; Unarmed for a punch).

  3. In the Attack with window, tick what applies in the Modifiers and choose a called shot if needed, then click Roll Dice.

The boxes follow the melee modifiers table (Core Rulebook p. 187): Attacker making charging attack (+2, and the running −2 does not apply), Attacker has superior position (+2), Attacker has friends in melee, Opponent prone, Attacker is using off-hand weapon, Touch-only attack… The Running box ticks itself when the token runs (@UUID[.AHFI77k4yz9xyzT4]{running}). Light and visibility count in melee as for shooting, wind does not (@UUID[.PweWVX3c5dHC50Ul]{the environment}).

An unarmed weapon can carry the Kick trait: a "Weapons / DV" effect aimed at Kick then only adds to it, without touching punches. That is what Satyr Legs need, +2 to kicking attacks (Run Faster p. 118).

Step by step: breaking free from a clinch or a pin

  1. In the header of the Martial Arts block, click the Escape (clinch or subdue) icon (①): it is a Complex Action, Unarmed Combat + Strength [Physical] (Run & Gun p. 122).

  2. The threshold is the hold's value. With grappling switched on, it fills itself in; otherwise, type it in the window.

  3. Roll. The card says "free" or "still clinched or pinned". With the Counter-grapple technique, a successful escape also offers to reverse the situation (Run & Gun p. 137-138).

Grappling tracking is a book option the GM switches on in Shadowrun settings, Combat tab: Use the grappling system (unticked by default, the page reloads). Unticked, nothing changes: escape keeps its threshold to type in, and the GM tracks grappling by hand.

Step by step: clinching an opponent (grappling on)

  1. Select your token, target the opponent in contact, then click the Clinch icon (②) of the Martial Arts block: Agility + Gymnastics [Physical] against Reaction + Intuition (Run & Gun p. 120).

  2. On the card, the defender clicks Defend. For an NPC, the GM first selects the defender's token: the defense against a clinch starts from the selected token.

  3. If the attacker wins by at least one hit, the defense card offers Clinch (hold: N): click. Both tokens carry the hold's state (Clinching an opponent and Clinched).

The hold is worth the net hits of the test that set it; it is the escape threshold. During a clinch, the one clinching has superior position (+2, ticked on its own), reach is cancelled between the two, and each suffers a penalty with their weapons: the melee weapon's reach, the hold's value with a weapon that shoots (Run & Gun p. 120-121).

  • Subdue (grappling): with an unarmed attack, this called shot without penalty deals no damage; if Strength and net hits exceed the defender's Physical limit, the card offers Pin down (Core Rulebook p. 194). The pinned character counts as prone for whoever attacks them.

  • Strengthen the hold (grappling), against your partner: net hits add to the hold, or reduce it if the defender wins (Core Rulebook p. 195).

  • Crush and Let go: buttons of the hold card, visible to the GM and to the one holding. Crushing deals Stun damage equal to Strength, without a test.

  • Reverse the situation: with the technique, the character held tries the reversal; successful, the roles swap (Run & Gun p. 112). The Counter-grapple and Reversal techniques come from the Mégapack.

The hold undoes itself when one of the two is unconscious or dead, at the end of combat, or when a token disappears. A hold weakened down to 0 stays in place: only escape frees (DjamZ's ruling).

All

What it is for

An attack is resolved in three chat cards: the attack, the target's defense, then resisting the damage. Each card carries the button for the next, reserved to whoever must click: the owner of the character targeted, or the GM for an NPC. At the end, a last button ticks the monitor's boxes, and the system draws the consequences: wound modifier, initiative, knockdown, unconsciousness.

Step by step: defending then resisting damage

  1. On the attack card, click Defend. The Defense Test window opens with Reaction + Intuition and the known modifiers.

  2. If needed, choose an active defense, cover or full defense (see below), then click Roll Dice.

  3. If the attacker wins, the defense card shows the Take On Damage button with the Damage Value and armor penetration: click it. The resistance window counts Body and armor, reduced by penetration (Core Rulebook p. 169-172).

  4. Roll, then click Apply Damage on the resistance card. The boxes are ticked, and the card shows "… damage applied".

If the defense wins, the card says Successful Defense and the exchange stops there. A target only defends once against the same attack: the button stays for the other targets, and the GM can reopen a defense by clicking themselves. An NPC's button belongs to the GM; it is reserved to the player for their character.

← @UUID[.WCNXngY9C9wo3kJa]{Related settings and references} · @UUID[.HxYeQa6b517Eo2te]{Defense options} →

• Cumulative defense (①): each defense already made in the Combat Turn removes one die from the next (Core Rulebook p. 189). The system counts on its own; the arrows icon resets the counter.

  • Active Defense (②): in melee, Block (Unarmed Combat, empty hands), Dodge (Gymnastics) or parry with a club or blade (Parry (Clubs), Parry (Blades)) adds the skill to the pool; against a shot, only dodging is possible. Each costs 5 Initiative points and only counts for this test (Core Rulebook p. 188, 190).

  • Cover: Partial Cover or Good Cover, to choose according to the scene; on a tie, the target is hit through its cover (Core Rulebook p. 188-190).

  • Full Defense (③): Willpower is added to all the character's defenses until the end of the Combat Turn, for 10 Initiative points (Core Rulebook p. 168, 190). The effect is set on the token and the points removed in the tracker.

The system refuses an active or full defense the Initiative Score can no longer pay for (the combined cost must be exceeded), and a parry or a block without the skill, as long as the Actions and initiative family of the locks is ticked (@UUID[.zazYeX6j2LJUFITG]{what costs initiative}). The Prone, Running and Receiving a charge boxes follow the defender's state; the penalties of a burst or a shotgun apply on their own according to the attack's firing mode (Core Rulebook p. 190); the card names the burst penalty.

Under suppressive fire: hitting the dirt

The card of a suppressive fire carries, next to Defend, the Hit the dirt button: instead of the Reaction + Edge test, the character drops prone with their Free Action if they have one left, otherwise with the "Hit the Dirt" interrupt (−5 initiative) (Core Rulebook p. 168, 181). They are prone (getting up costs a Simple Action) and still suffer the area's penalty. A character already on the ground who clicks Defend rolls nothing.

Caught in a net

A net lands on any successful attack, grazes included: the defense card carries Apply: caught in the net (threshold N), N being the net hits. The target is subdued (Core Rulebook p. 194) and counted as prone for the attacks aimed at it. Its card gives it Get free from the net: Complex Action, Unarmed Combat or Escape Artist + Agility [Physical], the better of the two, with −2 Agility in an XL net for a normal-size target and +2 for a troll in a standard net (Run & Gun p. 25, 28). A net without DV does no damage; the ShockNet is electrical, strikes even on a graze (Core Rulebook p. 173-174), and its second charge goes off at the start of the next turn if the target is still caught.

The penalty of suppressive fire applies to all the character's actions until the end of the Combat Turn, whether they are down or back up (Core Rulebook p. 180): getting up does not erase it. The roll window names it Special effect (Suppressive Fire).

Step by step: giving first aid

  1. Select the healer's token and target the wounded (that is the patient: without a target, the system takes the selected token).

  2. On the healer's sheet, skills tab, click First Aid.

  3. In the window, choose the Conditions (①), from Good (medical facility) to Terrible (gunfire, storm), and the Healing supplies (②): None, Improvised or Wireless medkit/autodoc. The patient's boxes (③) follow the healing modifiers table (Core Rulebook p. 207).

  4. Roll. The test is at threshold 2, and each hit beyond heals one box, without exceeding the First Aid rating (Core Rulebook p. 206): the card shows Heal N damage boxes, or a failure.

  5. Click the card's button. If the patient has two monitors, the system asks which one to heal.

First aid only applies once per set of wounds, and not after magical healing (Core Rulebook p. 206). A patient in full armor (Full armor box on the armor worn) only receives half the effects, rounded up. A critical glitch adds 1D3 boxes. First aid heals neither a device nor a drone.

Step by step: natural recovery

  1. On the wounded character's sheet, click the monitor's name, at the bottom: Stun or Physical (a right-click, on the other hand, resets the monitor).

  2. The healing window offers the same healing conditions; roll. It is an extended test: the card's New roll button rerolls, and the healing button unticks the boxes.

Stun heals before Physical: as long as the character has Stun damage, natural recovery of Physical is refused (Core Rulebook p. 206). The Medicine skill goes through the same window. Magical healing and the Heal spell are described with magic (@UUID[Compendium.sr5.manual.JournalEntry.jMw5X886fcLXtB6O.JournalEntryPage.L8wj3Cf3WQVKImL5]{casting a spell}) (Core Rulebook p. 209).

Healing under fire (Bullets & Bandages)

Two book options, unticked by default in Shadowrun settings, Body, health and augmentations tab: Healing under fire (a wound of 5 Physical boxes or more bleeds until stabilized; the first aid window offers Treatment, stabilization or Diagnosis) and Advanced medkits (Bullets & Bandages) (the medkit's rating in dice, one charge per patient) (Bullets & Bandages p. 14-19). The GM applies each bleeding box themselves, with a click on its card.

A toxin is a full-fledged item: the GM creates it, edits it and puts it on a weapon, a grenade or a critter's natural weapon. The Mégapack and the "[fr] Drogues" compendium provide some thirty of them, checked against the book; the Book toxins button, at the top of the Items tab (GM), creates the core rulebook's toxins in a folder of the world, without duplicates.

Step by step: poisoning a weapon (GM)

  1. Open the weapon's sheet, configuration tab: under the damage, a Drop a toxin from the world or a compendium here area is waiting.

  2. Drag the toxin there from the Items tab or a compendium. The weapon switches to Toxin damage and keeps a copy of its profile; the arrows resynchronize it after a change to the original toxin.

Step by step: resisting and applying

  1. The attack and the defense are played as usual. If the attack lands, the target clicks Resist toxin: Body + Willpower + the rating of their protection, each hit removing one point of Power (Core Rulebook p. 408). The Doses received at once field adds 1 Power per extra dose.

  2. The GM clicks Apply Toxin Effect when the indicated turn comes: damage and effects (disorientation, nausea, paralysis…) fall at once, and the special effect is shown as text.

A gas mask grants immunity to inhaled toxins, chemical seal to contact and inhaled ones, as long as the item is active; the message says what protected (Core Rulebook p. 408). Antidote patches (Chrome Flesh) remove their rating from the Power (Chrome Flesh p. 150). Diseases (a toxin that comes back, Pathogen box) and radiation are declared by the GM, then advance with the clock: see wiki: Toxins.

A drug goes into the sheet's gear. On its line, a single badge follows its phase.

Step by step: taking a drug

  1. Click the badge (②): the character takes the drug, one dose is removed and the effects of the high apply.

  2. Click again when the high ends: the crash effects replace those of the high.

  3. A last click ends the drug. A right-click by the GM resets it.

Taking a drug costs no action. An overdose opens the matching resistance window, and the addiction test follows the book (Core Rulebook p. 410-415); the Withdrawal: test modifier by level setting (Body, health and augmentations tab) quantifies the craving if the GM wishes.

Step by step: designing a drug

  1. Click Drug designer, at the top of the sidebar's Items tab: the button is there for the GM, and for the player whose character has the Chemistry skill (or when the GM has lifted the "Items" family of the locks). A list, at the top of the designer, chooses for which character; the GM also finds the world's items there. A player's request goes to the GM (Chrome Flesh p. 190-192).

  2. Choose the Base (①), then the level of each Block wanted (②), the Enhancers (③), the grade and the type of addiction. The result (effects, speed, duration, crash, addiction, availability, price) is computed as you go (Chrome Flesh p. 190-192).

  3. Click Create the drug. The GM's is created at once; the player's waits for the GM's validation, who receives it as a whisper with the Review the drug button.

A recipe contrary to the book is flagged in red and cannot be created. The crafting test (Chemistry + Logic) remains to be played by hand.

What it is for

Hiding a pistol under your jacket, frisking a suspect, picking a guard's pockets or slipping a tracker into a bag: the book settles them all with the same opposed test of Palming against Perception (Core Rulebook p. 420). The system plays it from start to finish, keeping it secret: the thief's roll and the target's go privately to the GM, and it is the GM who moves the item. Running, for its part, changes the dice of a whole Combat Turn: the system sets the state on the token and ticks the right boxes.

Step by step: concealing an item on yourself

  1. On the sheet, unfold the item's line by clicking its name (a weapon, a piece of armor, gear, a device).

  2. Click the Conceal on oneself tag (①): Palming + Agility [Physical], a Complex Action. The card is whispered to the GM.

  3. The item keeps its hits: a crossed-out eye follows its name on the sheet. To take it out, click the take-out button (Take out: …), or equip the weapon: a weapon in hand is never concealed.

Step by step: searching or frisking

  1. Target the token to examine.

  2. On the Perception line of the skills tab, click the magnifying glass (①) to look for a concealed item, or the hand (②) for a frisk, in contact. Choose the skill and, for a frisk, the attribute (Intuition or Agility).

  3. The GM receives the request and clicks Resolve: they tick the situation ("searching carefully", "distracted") and add a free modifier. The system rolls one test per hidden item.

An item is found if the searcher gets at least one hit and at least as many as whoever hid it: a tie goes to the searcher. In a frisk, a negative concealability is halved and a positive one doubled (Core Rulebook p. 420). The searcher only learns what they find; it is up to the GM to say whether they confiscate. Only items hidden with the button are searched for: a weapon simply worn under a coat is left to the GM's judgment.

Step by step: picking someone's pockets

  1. Select your token, then right-click the target, on a neighbouring square. The HUD opens on it even if you do not own it, with the Pickpocket hand (①) and, if you carry a small item, Plant an object (②).

  2. Click the hand. A window asks what you are after (optional: "his commlink", "at random"); this text will be shown on the card.

  3. Roll Palming + Agility [Physical]. The card goes privately to the GM: the target knows nothing. In combat, theft costs a Complex Action. Without Palming learned, the roll is refused (Core Rulebook p. 133).

Step by step: the GM's answer

  1. On the thief's card, click Target's Perception (button visible to the GM only).

  2. Choose the item (small ones first, or Random), the quantity for a stack, and the situation: Target distracted, Target watching their belongings, Diversion (Core Rulebook p. 135). Confirm the thief's hits.

  3. The system rolls the target's Perception + Intuition [Mental], with the item's concealability as a modifier, then offers the fitting button: Lift: … if the thief wins, Noticed: tell the target otherwise (a tie goes to the target).

Only small items (up to +2 concealability) can be stolen; an item stored in a locked container is not offered. With a glitch, the item goes through but the target feels something; on a critical glitch, the thief is caught red-handed. Planting an item follows the same path in the other direction. These follow-ups with no written rule are DjamZ's rulings, detailed on wiki: Pickpocketing.

House Rules

Pickpocketing: the thief chooses the object, Looting and spoils tab of Shadowrun settings, unticked by default (the book leaves the choice to the GM). Ticked, the thief chooses themselves, before their roll, among the target's small items; the GM keeps the Perception, the quantity and the transfer.

A character who goes beyond their walking rate is running until the end of the Combat Turn: +2 dice to their defenses, −2 to their actions, except Sprinting and charging (Core Rulebook p. 161-162, 176, 189).

Step by step: running

  1. Right-click your token and open the palette of movement types (the walker icon).

  2. Choose Run (①) or Sprint (②), then move the token. During a combat that has begun, it receives the Running state, which falls off on its own at the next Combat Turn or at the end of the encounter.

  3. To sprint further, roll the Sprint test from the sheet (movement block): Running + Strength [Physical], 2 m per hit (1 m for a dwarf or a troll).

As you drag the token, the path takes the colour of the pace, counting the meters already done in the turn: green up to walking, yellow up to running, red beyond. With the Running state, the roll window ticks on its own Running (−2) on actions, Attacker running on a shot and the +2 on defenses; nothing on Sprinting or on resistance tests. A melee attack's charge box removes the −2. All these boxes can still be unticked.

Running costs a Free Action per pass in which the token moves at a run (Core Rulebook p. 162). Each Sprint test made in combat in consecutive phases inflicts 1S fatigue, then 2S, 3S… resisted with Body + Willpower, without armor: it is the GM who sees the window open and rolls it (Core Rulebook p. 172).

What the system does on its own

  • It keeps the hits of a concealed item, rolls one test per item during a search and only shows the searcher what they find.

  • It routes the theft and its answer through the GM, recounts the hits announced and moves the item at the GM's click.

  • It sets and removes the Running state, ticks the running modifiers, counts down the Free Action and the sprint fatigue.

What the GM does by hand

  • Decides what a searcher confiscates, and about a weapon carried without having been hidden with the button.

  • Counts the fatigue of a long run outside combat, which is measured in minutes.
